transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I finally decided to make an appointment because... gosh, it’s just been really frustrating at work lately. I work as a receptionist and information clerk, you see, and usually, I pride myself on being very organized. I mean, you have to be in that role, right? You're the first face people see. 

But recently—and this is really what made me come in—I’ve started losing my place right in the middle of doing my normal, everyday tasks. Like, I’ll be on the computer scheduling appointments, and we get quite a lot of calls, so you really have to pay attention to the calendar, but my mind just completely slips off track. Or I’ll be out front working on the lobby displays, making sure all the informational brochures are perfectly aligned and up to date for the visitors, and suddenly I just totally blank on what I was doing. 

It’s like my brain just wanders off because I’m so busy thinking about what I might have overlooked. I’ll just be standing there holding a stack of pamphlets, completely derailed, running through a mental list of emails I might have forgotten to answer or small details I might have missed earlier in the morning, and I just can't seem to keep my focus on the thing right in front of me. It takes me so long just to reorient myself and figure out whose appointment I was trying to type in.
Have you been feeling sad or down lately?

No, I wouldn't say sad. I mean, I know sometimes people get depressed when they're stressed out, but that's really not it for me. It’s not a down feeling, you know? I don't wake up feeling hopeless or wanting to cry or anything like that. I actually have a pretty good life, and I genuinely like my job when I'm not, well, completely short-circuiting over the schedule. 

So no, not sad. It’s really just... I guess it's more of a constant, humming tension? Like, if you asked me if I was happy, I'd say yes, absolutely, but I'm just so preoccupied with all the things I need to manage. I remember just last weekend, my sister called and she actually asked if I was feeling down because I sounded so quiet and distracted on the phone. But I had to tell her, "No, I'm not sad, I'm just trying to remember if I locked the main filing cabinet before I left the front desk on Friday." 

So it's definitely not sadness at all, it's just... my brain just won't shut off about all those little details, so there's almost no room to even feel sad, if that makes sense.
Do you often feel anxious or nervous?

Oh, yes. Yes, definitely. I think nervous or anxious is exactly the right way to describe it. It’s like my mind is constantly spinning, and I find myself worrying about just... well, all kinds of ordinary things now. Things that really shouldn't be a big deal at all. 

Like, I mentioned the work schedules earlier, because that's a huge one for me at the desk, making sure everything is perfectly aligned so the day doesn't fall apart. But it’s not just work, it bleeds into everything else. I’ll be at home, and suddenly I’m agonizing over the bills. And not even because we can't pay them, but I'll start thinking, did I actually hit submit on the electric bill payment, or did I just close the browser tab? And then I have to go log back in to check, because I convince myself that if I missed it, they'll add a late fee, and then my credit score will drop, and it just spirals. 

Even things that are supposed to be fun are stressful now, like travel plans! We're supposed to go visit my husband's parents next month—just a short drive, really, maybe two hours—but I've been spending my whole evening stressing over whether we should leave at 8 AM or 9 AM to avoid traffic, and what if we hit construction, or what if I forget to pack the gift we bought them. 

And little paperwork errors, too. Like at the front desk, if I accidentally transpose two numbers on a patient's intake form... I mean, anyone could do that, right? It's a simple typo. But I'll sit there and worry that because of that one little mix-up, they won't get their follow-up call, and then it'll turn into this massive, horrible situation all because of me. It's just like every small, tiny thing feels like it could snowball into a much bigger problem, and I just can't seem to stop my brain from going down that path, no matter how much I try to rationalize it.
Do you experience any physical sensations, like a racing heart or trembling, when you're feeling anxious?

No, I really don't get anything like that. I know some people get the whole heart pounding out of their chest thing, or they start shaking, but I don't really have that. It's not a physical panic, if that makes sense. It's just all in my head. Like, I don't feel my heart racing when I'm worrying about the bills or the schedules or anything. It's just my thoughts racing, not my heart. 

I mean, I guess sometimes I might feel a little tense in my shoulders, just from sitting at the computer and being so focused on not making a mistake, but it's definitely not like a full-blown physical reaction. I don't get sweaty palms or feel like I can't breathe. It's just this constant mental loop. I'll just be sitting there, perfectly still, maybe a little stiff, but my brain is just going a mile a minute. So no, no trembling or anything like that. Just the worrying.
Is your worrying usually about a specific thing, like work or finances, or do you find yourself worrying about almost everything in general?

Well, it's really about everything, honestly. It's not just one specific thing like work or money, though those are definitely big ones, as I mentioned before. But it's like... it's like a net that just catches everything, you know? 

I could be worrying about the front desk schedule, and then the minute I finally get that sorted out in my head, I'm suddenly worrying about whether the dog has enough food for the week, even though I just bought a bag on Tuesday. Or I'll start thinking about my husband's commute and whether he remembered to check his tire pressure because it got a little cold last night. And then from there, it jumps to, oh, did I remember to RSVP to my niece's birthday party? And if I didn't, is my sister going to be mad at me? 

It's just this constant, rolling wave of things. I'll even worry about things that haven't happened yet, or things that probably won't ever happen. Like, last week I spent a good forty-five minutes just sitting on the couch, completely stressed out, because I started wondering what we would do if our water heater broke. It’s not old, it’s not making any weird noises, there is literally no reason to think it’s going to break. But my brain just decided, 'Hey, let's worry about a flooded basement today.' 

So, yeah, it’s definitely not just one or two things. It’s almost like my brain is just looking for a target, and once it finds one, it latches on, and then as soon as that's resolved, it just pivots to the very next thing on the list, no matter how small or random it is.
Has your worrying affected your relationships with family or friends?

No, I wouldn't say that. Not really, thankfully. I mean, my husband, he’s incredibly patient with me. He knows I get a little... well, he calls it getting 'wound up.' Like with the whole driving to his parents' house thing I was talking about? He just kind of sits back and lets me figure out the schedule. Sometimes I do wonder if he gets a tiny bit exhausted listening to me debate the pros and cons of leaving at 8 AM versus 9 AM for the fifth time in one night, but he never actually complains or gets frustrated with me. We’ve been married a long time, so he’s just used to my... my process, I guess you could call it. 

And as for my friends, or my sister—who I see pretty often—I mostly just keep it all inside when I’m around them. Like, we could be sitting there having lunch, and my brain is doing that whole spinning thing, worrying about whether I remembered to lock the filing cabinet at the front desk or if I paid that electric bill, but I don't usually say it out loud. I just smile and nod and keep eating my salad. So she probably doesn't even know I’m worrying half the time! I try really, really hard not to put it on other people, you know? It feels like it’s my own brain doing this, so why bother them with it? 

So, no, there haven't been any big arguments or people pulling away from me or anything dramatic like that. It’s really just a burden on me, honestly, because I’m the one who has to listen to my own thoughts all day. I do wonder sometimes if they notice me zoning out when I’m caught up in one of my little worry loops, but no one has ever said anything to me about it affecting them, so I think my relationships are perfectly fine.
Do you worry about your health as well?

No, not really. I mean, I don't sit around worrying that I have some terrible disease or anything like that. I know some people get a headache and immediately think it's a brain tumor, but I'm not like that at all. 

I mean, sure, I'll worry about things like, did I drink enough water today? Because sometimes if I get busy at the desk, I'll realize at 3 PM that I've only had one cup of coffee and no water, and then I'll worry that I'm going to get dehydrated and get a headache, which would make it hard to focus on the afternoon schedule. But that's more of a practical worry, you know? It's not like I think I'm going to drop dead from dehydration. 

And I guess I worry about getting a cold, especially in the winter, because if I get sick, I have to call out of work, and finding coverage for the front desk is always a nightmare. The last time I had a cold, it took three phone calls just to get someone to cover my morning shift, and I spent the whole time I was supposed to be resting just stressing about whether they were handling the phones right. But again, that's really more about the logistics of being sick and how it messes up the schedule, rather than an actual fear for my health. 

I do try to eat relatively healthy and I take a multivitamin, but I don't obsess over every little ache or pain. Like, if my knee hurts, I just figure I sat funny in my chair, I don't go spiraling into thinking I need a knee replacement. So, no, health isn't really one of the things that gets caught in that net I was talking about. It's mostly just the day-to-day stuff, the schedules, the bills, making sure everything is running smoothly. My actual health is probably the one thing I don't overthink!
Are you having trouble sleeping at night due to your worrying?

Oh, yes. That is... honestly, that's probably the most frustrating part of my entire day. Because the thing is, most nights I get into bed and I am just so, so tired. I mean, after sitting at the front desk for eight hours, dealing with the phones ringing off the hook and managing the waiting room, my body is just completely exhausted. I'll do my whole nighttime routine, wash my face, maybe read a chapter of a book to try and wind down, and I feel totally ready to sleep. 

But the absolute second I turn off the lamp and close my eyes, it's like my brain decides it's time for a second shift. I'll just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and suddenly I'm going over tomorrow's appointments in my head. I'll start wondering if I accidentally double-booked the 10 AM slot, or I'll panic about some intake form I might have missed filing before I locked up. Like, I'll literally try to visualize my desk in the dark to remember if I put the blue folder in the outgoing tray or if I accidentally left it sitting by the keyboard, because if I left it out, it's going to mess up the flow for the medical assistants the next morning. 

And it just goes on and on like that. I'll toss and turn, just mentally organizing the schedule and second-guessing everything I did that day. And the worst part is, even when I finally do manage to fall asleep—because eventually my body just gives out, right?—it doesn't even feel like real, restful sleep. When my alarm goes off at six, I wake up feeling like I never really settled. It's like my brain kept running the front desk all night long while I was unconscious, and I just wake up feeling completely unrefreshed, like I didn't get a break from my own thoughts at all. It makes the mornings really tough, honestly.
Are there any activities or tasks outside of work that you've stopped doing or are avoiding because of your worrying?

Outside of work? No, not really. I mean, I still go to the grocery store and run my errands and do all my normal household stuff. I haven't stopped doing anything at home. But, you know, it's funny you ask about tasks, because where I really, really notice it affecting what I do is actually *at* work. I know you asked about outside the office, but it's just been bothering me so much lately and it's kind of bleeding into everything. 

I’m still showing up every day and getting through the day, I really am. I haven't called out or let the front desk fall apart. But the scheduling... oh my goodness, the scheduling takes me so much longer now. I used to just breeze right through it, you know? Someone calls, I click the 2:15 slot, save it, and move on. Now, because my mind is always spinning and I'm so worried about messing up the doctors' days, I double-check myself so much. I'll put a patient in, and then two seconds later I'll think, 'Wait, did I put them on Tuesday or Thursday?' Even though I *just* did it! So I have to open the calendar back up, verify the date, verify the provider, and then I worry I accidentally clicked and dragged their appointment to the wrong time while I was checking, so I have to check it a third time! It just eats up so much of my morning. 

And it's not just the computer stuff, either. Part of my job is keeping the waiting room looking nice and organized, and recently I’ve actually had to redo parts of the lobby displays. I'll be out there arranging the informational pamphlets or updating the little corkboard with the seasonal flu shot reminders, and my mind will just start racing about some insurance intake form or whether I locked the filing cabinet. Next thing I know, I've completely lost track of what I was arranging. I'll look down and realize I put all the pediatric brochures in the adult wellness slots, or I pinned the flyers up all out of order, and I have to take it all down and start completely over. I spent twenty minutes fixing a magazine rack last week because I just kept zoning out. So, I haven't stopped doing my tasks, it's just... everything feels like it takes twice the effort now because my brain won't just let me do a simple task once and be done with it.
Do you feel like your worrying is interfering with your ability to enjoy your job or perform it as well as you used to?

Oh, absolutely. The enjoyment is... well, it's pretty much completely gone at this point, which is really sad for me to admit. I mean, I used to really love my job. I've always been a people person, you know? I always liked being the first face people saw when they walked into the clinic, making them feel welcome, especially since going to the doctor can be stressful for people. 

And as for performing it, like I was saying with the scheduling taking me twice as long, I am still getting the work done. I can still put on that professional front. At the front desk, I can still smile and help people, I can hand them their clipboards and cheerfully explain their copays. If you just looked at me from the waiting room, you'd probably think I was doing just fine and everything was completely normal. 

But inside... oh, inside it is a completely different story. I just feel so, so wound tight all day long. It's like my body is constantly bracing for an impact that never comes. I'll be sitting there typing, smiling at a patient, and I'll suddenly realize that my shoulders are practically up around my ears. Like, physically, I am just carrying so much tension in my neck and my back all day. I'll try to consciously take a deep breath and drop my shoulders down, but five minutes later, I'm right back to being this tightly coiled spring. 

And it's just this constant, exhausting feeling that I’m waiting for something to go wrong. Every single time the phone rings, instead of just thinking, 'Oh, I need to answer that,' my heart gives this little jump, and my brain instantly goes, 'Who is calling to complain? Did I mess up a referral? Did I send someone to the wrong office?' It really ruins the day-to-day enjoyment, because you can't really enjoy chatting with a patient or joking with the medical assistants when your whole body feels like it's vibrating with stress, you know? I just sit there, pleasant on the outside, but inside I'm just so incredibly tense, just waiting for the other shoe to drop.
Do you feel like your worrying is affecting your relationships with your husband or other family members in any significant way?

My husband? No, honestly, I really don't think so. I mean, we've been married for eighteen years now, and he is just... he's very steady, you know? A very go-with-the-flow kind of person, which is honestly a blessing because if we were both wound up like I've been lately, I don't know how we'd function. 

When I get home—usually I pull into the driveway around 5:45, unless the traffic on the highway is backed up, which it has been almost every day this month because of that awful bridge repair they're doing—I walk in and he's usually already got dinner started or he's just relaxing in the living room. And I might vent for a few minutes about how the phones wouldn't stop ringing or how the schedule got all messed up, but he just kind of nods and listens. He's really good like that. He doesn't take it personally if I come through the door looking a little frazzled.

And as for the rest of the family, my sister lives out of state, so we mostly just talk on Sunday afternoons, and that's always fine. We just chat about her kids and my week, so there's no real strain there. So, no, my husband and I aren't arguing more or anything like that. I don't think my worrying is causing any friction between us. 

I do feel a little guilty sometimes, though, because like I was saying before, I'm just so exhausted by the time I get home that I'm not exactly the life of the party. We'll sit down on the couch after dinner to watch TV—we've been watching this new mystery series he likes—and I'm just kind of sitting there like a lump, trying to unwind my shoulders and trying so hard not to think about the clinic's appointment book for the next morning. But he doesn't seem to mind that I'm a little quiet. He knows I work hard. So, no, I wouldn't say it's affecting my marriage or my family in any big way. The stress really just stays trapped inside my own head, or it comes out when I'm sitting at that front desk. At home, things are pretty much okay.
Are you finding it difficult to enjoy activities or hobbies that you used to find pleasurable outside of your job?

Oh, no, not at all. Actually, my hobbies are kind of my saving grace right now. I've always been a really big gardener, you know? I have these raised beds out in the backyard that my husband built for me about five years ago... no, wait, it was six years ago, right before we got that really bad ice storm. Anyway, I still absolutely love getting out there on a Saturday morning. There's just something about having my hands in the dirt that really grounds me, I think. 

I've been growing heirloom tomatoes this year—specifically these Cherokee Purples, which are honestly so finicky but they are just so delicious if you can get the soil pH just right. I also have some zucchini, which always overproduces, and a whole little herb garden by the back steps. When I'm out there pulling weeds or pruning the tomato vines, I can actually just focus on the plants. I don't think about the clinic's schedule or the phone ringing or whether I filed those charts correctly. It's just me and the garden, and I still get so much joy out of seeing the first little green tomatoes pop up. 

And then on Sundays, I usually do a lot of baking. I've been really into making sourdough bread, which I know became such a huge fad for everyone a few years ago, but I actually stuck with it! Keeping the starter alive is almost like having a pet, you know? You have to feed it on a schedule and make sure the water temperature is exactly right. And the kneading process—oh, kneading the dough is actually wonderful for all that physical tension in my shoulders and my back that I was telling you about earlier. I can just stand at the kitchen island and push all my stress right into the dough for ten solid minutes. 

So, no, I haven't lost interest in my hobbies or anything like that. If anything, I look forward to them even more now because they're the only times my brain finally gets a little bit of quiet and I can just be myself. I just wish I could figure out a way to bottle up that feeling and bring it with me to the front desk on Monday mornings, you know? But at home, doing my own things, I still really enjoy all of it.
Do you feel like your worrying is significantly interfering with your daily life or causing you a lot of distress?

Well, distress, yes, absolutely. The internal stress is just a lot, like I was describing with my shoulders and that constant waiting for the other shoe to drop. But as far as actually interfering with my daily life... it's kind of a yes and no situation. 

I mean, I’m still showing up and getting through the day. I haven't called out sick or missed a shift at all, not even when I had this awful sinus thing back in February. I still get up, put on my uniform, drive in, and get the work done. So from the outside, I'm functioning. 

But... well, like I was mentioning earlier about the scheduling, it just takes me so much longer now. I used to be able to just type in a patient's name, book their follow-up for three weeks out, and boom, done in thirty seconds. Now, I double-check myself so much. I'll click the appointment, make sure it's the right provider—because we have two Dr. Smiths in our network, you know, one is cardiology and one is internal medicine, which is a terrible system if you ask me—and I'll check the date, and then I'll check it again, and maybe a third time, just terrified I'm going to put them on the wrong day and they'll show up and be angry with me. It just drags everything out.

And it's not just the computer work, either. It's the little physical tasks around the clinic, too. Like, just the other day, I was working on the lobby displays. We have this big rack of informational pamphlets near the water cooler, and I was trying to organize them because we just got all these new ones in about flu season and winter wellness. But my mind was just spinning so fast about whether I'd forgotten to fax a prior authorization that morning that I completely lost track of what I was arranging. I ended up putting the pediatrics brochures mixed in with the Medicare information, and the whole thing was just a jumbled mess. I literally had to pull everything out and redo parts of the lobby displays all over again because I just couldn't keep my focus on what my hands were doing. 

So, it's things like that. I'm getting the job done, eventually, but it's just taking so much more mental energy and time than it ever used to, and it is just incredibly frustrating to feel like I can't just do my normal, everyday routine without second-guessing every single little move I make.
Are there any situations or tasks that you avoid because they might trigger or worsen your worrying?

Avoid? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, I really wish I could sometimes! But no, I don't actually avoid anything. 

Take the phones at work, for instance. On Monday mornings, right at 8:00 AM when the lines open, all four lines on my console will light up at the exact same time. It's like everyone in town decided to get sick over the weekend or suddenly remembered they need a refill right this second. And I sit there, and my stomach just kind of drops, and I think, "I really don't want to pick this up." Because you just never know who is going to be on the other end of the line, you know? It could be someone yelling about a prior authorization that their insurance denied, or someone who's really upset, and it definitely makes my worrying spike just looking at those blinking red lights. I'll sit there and think about all the ways the call could go wrong before I even say hello.

But I don't avoid it. I can't, right? It's my job. I'm the one at the front desk, so if I don't answer it by the third ring, it rolls over to the back office, and the nurses get so incredibly annoyed when that happens because they're busy doing vitals and rooming patients. They've complained about it in staff meetings before, and I am not going to be the reason they get behind. So I just take a deep breath and pick up the receiver. 

And it's the same thing outside of work, too. Like going to the grocery store. I really hate going to the grocery store on Sunday afternoons because it is always so packed, and I get so worried about forgetting something important for the week's dinners, or I'll start stressing about whether I bought enough of the right snacks for my husband's lunches. I'll stand in the produce section just agonizing over whether to get the bagged spinach or the fresh heads of lettuce, worrying that one will go bad before we eat it. But I still go. I get my cart, I walk down every single aisle with my list, and I get it done. 

So, no, I don't think I actually avoid any situations or tasks. I don't hide from things. I just... I do it all, I just worry the entire time I'm doing it, if that makes sense. I just push through the stress because things have to get done.
Are you finding it harder to concentrate on tasks outside of work due to your worrying?

Outside of work? Um, actually, no, not really. Like I was saying earlier with the gardening and the sourdough bread, when I'm at home doing my own hobbies, I can usually lock right in and just focus on what's in front of me. It's really just at the clinic where my concentration completely falls apart. 

In fact, that’s honestly what made me finally decide I needed to make this appointment and come in to see you. It's gotten to the point where I’ve started just... losing my place right in the middle of doing my normal duties. Like when I’m scheduling appointments, or like I mentioned before with working on the lobby displays. I'll be right in the middle of typing in a patient's details or sorting through those brochures, and my mind just completely slips off track. I'll just freeze, staring at the computer screen or the pamphlet rack, because my brain is suddenly a million miles away, busy thinking about what I might have overlooked earlier in the morning. 

I'll be sitting there wondering, did I send that referral? Did I check the right box on that insurance form? Did I put that one patient on the wrong Dr. Smith's schedule? And because I'm so wrapped up in trying to figure out if I missed something important, I completely lose my train of thought on the task I'm actually trying to finish. It's just so frustrating because I've always prided myself on being so sharp and on top of things at the front desk, and now I'm standing there totally blanking on what my hands were doing just two seconds prior because my brain won't stop running down a list of everything I might have forgotten.
Are there any tasks or activities that you used to do but have stopped doing because of your worrying?

Stopped doing? Um... no. No, I haven't stopped doing anything at all, really. 

Like I was saying about the sourdough and the gardening, I still do all of that. I mean, the sourdough alone is a huge commitment, right? You have to feed the starter every single day, and you have to make sure your kitchen is the exact right temperature—if it drops below 70 degrees, the yeast just gets so sluggish, and then I start worrying that I've completely killed it and wasted all that flour. Flour is so expensive right now, too, especially the good artisan bread flour I like to get from that little mill one town over. But even though I stress about ruining the batch or timing the proofing wrong because my mind is elsewhere, I still bake every single week. I haven't given it up.

And the same goes for the gardening. I was just out there on Saturday, pulling weeds around the heirloom tomatoes. I worry constantly that the aphids are going to get them, or that I'm overwatering and causing root rot, but I don't just abandon the garden. I still get out there with my trowel and my gloves and I get my hands dirty. 

I guess I've just never been the type of person to quit things. My mom raised my sister and me to just push through whatever was bothering us, so even though my mind is constantly running through all these worst-case scenarios and I feel all this tension, I just keep pushing forward. I still do all the cooking, the cleaning, the grocery shopping, my job at the clinic... I haven't dropped a single responsibility or hobby. It's just that now, doing all those things comes with this heavy, exhausting layer of worry on top of it. But to answer your question, no, I haven't actually stopped doing anything.
Are there any tasks or situations that you're avoiding because you worry about how they might turn out?

Well, like I was saying before about avoiding things... no, not really. I mean, I definitely worry about how things will turn out all the time, constantly, actually. But I don't avoid them. 

Take the staff scheduling at the clinic, for example. We just had to do the holiday schedule for November and December, and it is always a complete nightmare. Everyone wants the day after Thanksgiving off, everyone wants Christmas Eve off, and nobody wants to work the late shift on New Year's Eve. And because I'm the senior receptionist, our office manager, Linda—she's been there for like fifteen years and just hates dealing with conflict—she hands the blank grid over to me and asks me to "draft" it. 

I agonize over it. I literally take the spreadsheet home and sit at my kitchen table with a pencil and a huge eraser, and my stomach is just in knots. I worry that if I give Sarah the Friday off, then Jessica is going to be furious because she asked for it three months ago, but Sarah has seniority, so technically she should get it. But then Jessica has that new baby, and daycare is closed, so if I schedule her, she might just call out sick anyway, which leaves us short-staffed at the front desk. And then the phones will be ringing off the hook, like I told you about, and the nurses will get mad. I sit there and play out every single scenario, worrying that no matter what I do, someone is going to be mad at me or the clinic is going to fall apart. 

It takes me hours to do a schedule that should take twenty minutes because I'm so paralyzed by worrying about the outcome. But I still do it. I fill out the grid, I hand it back to Linda, and I post it in the breakroom. I don't avoid doing it, even though I absolutely dread it and it makes my chest feel incredibly tight the entire week I'm working on it. So, no, I'm not avoiding anything. I just suffer through it, I guess.
Are you finding that your worrying is significantly impacting your ability to perform your job or maintain your relationships?

Well, I guess... I mean, I'm still showing up. I'm there every day at 7:45 AM, unlocking the front doors, turning on the lights in the waiting room, making the coffee for the staff breakroom... I haven't missed a single day of work. And my relationships, well, I still call my sister every Sunday evening, and my husband and I still have our usual routine, though he does tell me I seem distracted a lot lately. 

But as far as my job goes... it is definitely impacting things, even if I'm still getting through the day. Like I was saying about the scheduling, right? It just takes me so much longer now. I used to just breeze through the daily appointment confirmations, but now I find myself double-checking and triple-checking everything. I'll look at a patient's chart, see that they're confirmed for 2:00 PM with Dr. Evans, and then I'll second-guess myself. Did I actually read that right? Did I accidentally look at Tuesday's schedule instead of Wednesday's? So I'll close the window, open it back up, check the date, check the doctor's name, check the patient's date of birth... just to be absolutely sure I didn't mess it up. It slows me down so much, and then the phones start backing up.

And it's not just the computer work. It's the physical stuff, too. Like those lobby displays I mentioned earlier. We have this big bulletin board where we pin up all the seasonal health information—flu shots in the fall, allergy tips in the spring, sun safety in the summer. I was redoing it last week for the upcoming winter season, putting up all these flyers about handwashing and cold symptoms. I had all the pamphlets laid out on the counter, categorized by topic, and I was right in the middle of pinning them up... and my brain just went completely sideways worrying about whether I had remembered to fax over a prior authorization for a patient's MRI. I just stood there holding a pushpin and a flyer about the flu vaccine, completely lost. By the time I snapped out of it, I had totally lost track of what I was arranging. I had to pull half the flyers down and completely redo that section of the board because I had put the pediatric stuff mixed in with the geriatric stuff, and it looked like a total mess. 

So, yes, I'm getting the job done eventually, but it's like wading through molasses. Everything just takes so much more effort and so much more time because I'm constantly having to backtrack and fix things after my mind wanders off into this panic about what I might have done wrong.

I get my cart, I walk down every single aisle with my list, and I get it done. 

So, no, I don't think I actually avoid any situations or tasks. I don't hide from things. I just... I do it all, I just worry the entire time I'm doing it, if that makes sense. I just push through the stress because things have to get done.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's worrying is causing significant impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Are you finding it harder to concentrate on tasks outside of work due to your worrying?

target_item.name: Concentration_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: What made me come in is that I’ve started losing my place while I’m scheduling appointments or working on the lobby displays, like my mind slips off track because I’m busy thinking about what I might have overlooked.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty concentrating, which corresponds to the symptom of concentration difficulty, even though they specifically asked about outside of work.

patient.answer:
Outside of work? Um, actually, no, not really. Like I was saying earlier with the gardening and the sourdough bread, when I'm at home doing my own hobbies, I can usually lock right in and just focus on what's in front of me. It's really just at the clinic where my concentration completely falls apart. 

In fact, that’s honestly what made me finally decide I needed to make this appointment and come in to see you. It's gotten to the point where I’ve started just... losing my place right in the middle of doing my normal duties. Like when I’m scheduling appointments, or like I mentioned before with working on the lobby displays. I'll be right in the middle of typing in a patient's details or sorting through those brochures, and my mind just completely slips off track. I'll just freeze, staring at the computer screen or the pamphlet rack, because my brain is suddenly a million miles away, busy thinking about what I might have overlooked earlier in the morning. 

I'll be sitting there wondering, did I send that referral? Did I check the right box on that insurance form? Did I put that one patient on the wrong Dr. Smith's schedule? And because I'm so wrapped up in trying to figure out if I missed something important, I completely lose my train of thought on the task I'm actually trying to finish. It's just so frustrating because I've always prided myself on being so sharp and on top of things at the front desk, and now I'm standing there totally blanking on what my hands were doing just two seconds prior because my brain won't stop running down a list of everything I might have forgotten.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing significant avoidance behaviors
doctor.question: Are there any tasks or activities that you used to do but have stopped doing because of your worrying?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoidance or stopping activities due to worry, which is not a specific symptom in the patient's profile (the patient's functional impairment does not include stopping activities, but rather taking longer and redoing tasks).

patient.answer:
Stopped doing? Um... no. No, I haven't stopped doing anything at all, really. 

Like I was saying about the sourdough and the gardening, I still do all of that. I mean, the sourdough alone is a huge commitment, right? You have to feed the starter every single day, and you have to make sure your kitchen is the exact right temperature—if it drops below 70 degrees, the yeast just gets so sluggish, and then I start worrying that I've completely killed it and wasted all that flour. Flour is so expensive right now, too, especially the good artisan bread flour I like to get from that little mill one town over. But even though I stress about ruining the batch or timing the proofing wrong because my mind is elsewhere, I still bake every single week. I haven't given it up.

And the same goes for the gardening. I was just out there on Saturday, pulling weeds around the heirloom tomatoes. I worry constantly that the aphids are going to get them, or that I'm overwatering and causing root rot, but I don't just abandon the garden. I still get out there with my trowel and my gloves and I get my hands dirty. 

I guess I've just never been the type of person to quit things. My mom raised my sister and me to just push through whatever was bothering us, so even though my mind is constantly running through all these worst-case scenarios and I feel all this tension, I just keep pushing forward. I still do all the cooking, the cleaning, the grocery shopping, my job at the clinic... I haven't dropped a single responsibility or hobby. It's just that now, doing all those things comes with this heavy, exhausting layer of worry on top of it. But to answer your question, no, I haven't actually stopped doing anything.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing significant avoidance behaviors
doctor.question: Are there any tasks or situations that you're avoiding because you worry about how they might turn out?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoidance behavior, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was saying before about avoiding things... no, not really. I mean, I definitely worry about how things will turn out all the time, constantly, actually. But I don't avoid them. 

Take the staff scheduling at the clinic, for example. We just had to do the holiday schedule for November and December, and it is always a complete nightmare. Everyone wants the day after Thanksgiving off, everyone wants Christmas Eve off, and nobody wants to work the late shift on New Year's Eve. And because I'm the senior receptionist, our office manager, Linda—she's been there for like fifteen years and just hates dealing with conflict—she hands the blank grid over to me and asks me to "draft" it. 

I agonize over it. I literally take the spreadsheet home and sit at my kitchen table with a pencil and a huge eraser, and my stomach is just in knots. I worry that if I give Sarah the Friday off, then Jessica is going to be furious because she asked for it three months ago, but Sarah has seniority, so technically she should get it. But then Jessica has that new baby, and daycare is closed, so if I schedule her, she might just call out sick anyway, which leaves us short-staffed at the front desk. And then the phones will be ringing off the hook, like I told you about, and the nurses will get mad. I sit there and play out every single scenario, worrying that no matter what I do, someone is going to be mad at me or the clinic is going to fall apart. 

It takes me hours to do a schedule that should take twenty minutes because I'm so paralyzed by worrying about the outcome. But I still do it. I fill out the grid, I hand it back to Linda, and I post it in the breakroom. I don't avoid doing it, even though I absolutely dread it and it makes my chest feel incredibly tight the entire week I'm working on it. So, no, I'm not avoiding anything. I just suffer through it, I guess.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing significant impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Are you finding that your worrying is significantly impacting your ability to perform your job or maintain your relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up and getting through the day, but scheduling takes me longer now because I double-check myself so much, and I’ve had to redo parts of the lobby displays after losing track of what I was arranging.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of the worry on the patient's ability to perform her job or maintain relationships, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment item.

patient.answer:
Well, I guess... I mean, I'm still showing up. I'm there every day at 7:45 AM, unlocking the front doors, turning on the lights in the waiting room, making the coffee for the staff breakroom... I haven't missed a single day of work. And my relationships, well, I still call my sister every Sunday evening, and my husband and I still have our usual routine, though he does tell me I seem distracted a lot lately. 

But as far as my job goes... it is definitely impacting things, even if I'm still getting through the day. Like I was saying about the scheduling, right? It just takes me so much longer now. I used to just breeze through the daily appointment confirmations, but now I find myself double-checking and triple-checking everything. I'll look at a patient's chart, see that they're confirmed for 2:00 PM with Dr. Evans, and then I'll second-guess myself. Did I actually read that right? Did I accidentally look at Tuesday's schedule instead of Wednesday's? So I'll close the window, open it back up, check the date, check the doctor's name, check the patient's date of birth... just to be absolutely sure I didn't mess it up. It slows me down so much, and then the phones start backing up.

And it's not just the computer work. It's the physical stuff, too. Like those lobby displays I mentioned earlier. We have this big bulletin board where we pin up all the seasonal health information—flu shots in the fall, allergy tips in the spring, sun safety in the summer. I was redoing it last week for the upcoming winter season, putting up all these flyers about handwashing and cold symptoms. I had all the pamphlets laid out on the counter, categorized by topic, and I was right in the middle of pinning them up... and my brain just went completely sideways worrying about whether I had remembered to fax over a prior authorization for a patient's MRI. I just stood there holding a pushpin and a flyer about the flu vaccine, completely lost. By the time I snapped out of it, I had totally lost track of what I was arranging. I had to pull half the flyers down and completely redo that section of the board because I had put the pediatric stuff mixed in with the geriatric stuff, and it looked like a total mess. 

So, yes, I'm getting the job done eventually, but it's like wading through molasses. Everything just takes so much more effort and so much more time because I'm constantly having to backtrack and fix things after my mind wanders off into this panic about what I might have done wrong.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of excessive and persistent worry about everyday things, such as work, finances, and minor details, along with feelings of tension and difficulty concentrating, are consistent with Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD). The patient's worry is also causing significant distress and impairment in their daily life, particularly at work.
